title: Speak good
hook: praising others is part of guarding speech

segments.voice: Yesterday: listening counts too. Your line was don't listen. Did you get to use your exit? After days of what not to say, a new week begins, and the tongue gets a job. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-five.

A teacher sits with his students and describes them, one by one. Of the first he says: a plastered cistern that never loses a drop. Of another: happy is the one who gave birth to him. Of another: a man of piety. Another: one who fears sin. And of the last: a spring that keeps on flowing, getting stronger as it goes. The teacher is Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, and the scene is preserved in Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers. It's a report card with no grades on it. Only praise, each piece cut to fit one person.
screen: `A TEACHER DESCRIBES HIS STUDENTS.` → `A CISTERN, A SPRING.` → `ONLY PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Speak good. Turn it four ways. First, the habit. Avot doesn't say he praised them once. It says he used to recount their praise. Praise as a practice, something a teacher did on purpose, the way someone else might keep a journal. After days of everything the tongue shouldn't do, here is something it should. Guarding speech isn't only a wall; it's also a road. Second, the shape of good praise. Notice that no two students get the same line. The cistern is for a student who remembered everything he learned. The flowing spring is for a student whose ideas kept coming. That's praise that has actually looked at someone. "Great job" is kind. "You never lose a drop" is seen. Third, a caution, because the tradition is careful even here. The Talmud warns that praising someone at length can backfire: talk long enough about someone's good side and somebody in the room will start listing the other side. Maimonides adds that praising a person in front of people who dislike them is a kind of shadow of lashon hara, because it invites the attack. So the tradition's version of speaking good has judgment in it: honest, specific, and said where it builds rather than where it provokes. Fourth, the absent. Gossip is talk about someone who isn't in the room. Praise can be too. Saying something good about a person who will never hear it isn't flattery, since there's nothing to gain. It simply puts their good name back into circulation, the opposite of a cut-open pillow.
screen: `HE USED TO RECOUNT THEIR PRAISE.` · `A CISTERN, A SPRING: PRAISE THAT SEES.` · `PRAISE WITH JUDGMENT.` · `PRAISE THE ONE WHO ISN'T THERE.` · then, large: `SPEAK GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: praise someone who isn't there. Settle, and breathe. Choose a person who won't be in the room with you today. A coworker, a sibling, a neighbor, a teacher from long ago. Look at them the way Rabban Yochanan looked at his students. What is true and particular about them? Not "nice," not "great." Find the image. The one who always remembers. The one whose kindness keeps flowing. Shape it into a single sentence you could say about them to someone else. Hold it until it feels honest. If you pray, you can give thanks for that person in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Speak good. In Jewish teaching, guarding speech includes honest, specific praise of others, said with judgment, as Rabban Yochanan praised his students. Today's word.
Your line: speak good. Today, say the sentence you found about someone who isn't there, to someone who is. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Jews study Pirkei Avot, including Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's praise of his students; teachers of speech present honest praise of others as part of guarding the tongue, with care not to praise in a way that provokes criticism.

myth: guarding speech only means staying quiet
Avot shows a teacher who made praise a habit: speech has a job, not just a wall.
Rabban Yochanan gave each student the same praise
each got his own image: a cistern, a spring, piety, fear of sin.
the tradition warns that praise can backfire
praising at length, or before people who dislike someone, can invite criticism of them.

fork.setup: you're with colleagues who can't stand a coworker, and you think she did excellent work this week. what do you do?
options: praise her at length right now.
save the praise for a place where it builds her up.
fork.reveal: Maimonides calls praise in front of someone's detractors a shadow of lashon hara: it invites the attack. speak good, with judgment.

trapdoor: what you thought: guarding your tongue means saying less.
what it means: it also means saying good things, honestly and specifically.
what a scholar hears: Avot shows Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai recounting his students' praise, while the Talmud and Maimonides warn that praise in the wrong setting can lead to disparagement.

notes: Avot 2:8 (numbering varies by edition, 2:8–2:9 or 2:10–2:11): Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's praise of his disciples, paraphrased. The disciples are not named in the voice; images: plastered cistern (Eliezer ben Hyrcanus), 'happy is she who bore him' (Joshua ben Chananiah), pious (Yose the Priest), fearer of sin (Shimon ben Netanel), ever-strengthening spring (Elazar ben Arach). Confirm the paraphrases and the reading of the cistern/spring images.
Arakhin 16a (also Bava Batra 164b): one should not speak at length in praise of another, as it leads to disparagement. Confirm citation.
Maimonides, Hilchot De'ot 7:4: praising someone before his enemies is 'avak lashon hara' (rendered 'a shadow of lashon hara'). Confirm.
Number of disciples deliberately not stated.
